gates.action: Take another photo in better light
gates.text: The photo was too unclear to read the packaging properly. A verdict built on a photo this poor would not be worth trusting, so nothing is decided from it.
The material could not be identified with enough confidence. Every rule here turns on what the item is made of, so without that there is nothing to apply.

gates.action: Separate the parts if you can, then check each one
gates.text: Two or more materials are joined together. Recycling handles each material separately, and the Plastic Waste Management Rules single out multilayered packaging as its own category for exactly this reason.

gates.action: Clean it out, then look again
gates.text: Too much food or liquid is left inside. Dry waste has to be kept clean and dry to be worth recycling, and heavily soiled packaging is usually rejected.

Every written check passed, but a model trained on our own photos of damaged packaging judged this reading itself too unreliable to decide on. The model can only ever hold an answer back, never give one, so no rule here was overruled.

rules.action: Check how thick it is before deciding
rules.text: Thin plastic film, such as a carry bag or a wrapper, turns on its thickness rather than its resin. The Plastic Waste Management Rules ban carry bags below the minimum thickness rather than recycling them, and film is sorted separately from rigid plastic, so this one cannot be called from the material alone.

rules.action: Dry waste, but not for recycling
rules.text: Expanded polystyrene foam is almost entirely air, so collecting and carrying it costs more than the plastic ever recovered from it. Very few recyclers take it.

rules.action: Dry waste, but not for recycling
rules.text: Polystyrene, resin code 6, is seldom accepted for recycling in India. It still belongs with your dry waste rather than your wet waste, but do not expect it to be recycled.
PET, resin code 1, is the most widely recycled plastic in India. Empty it and keep it with your dry waste.
High density polyethylene, resin code 2, the plastic of milk and detergent bottles, is readily recycled. Empty it and keep it with your dry waste.
Low density polyethylene, resin code 4, in a solid form such as a squeeze bottle or a lid, is a recyclable plastic under the resin codes the Plastic Waste Management Rules use.
Polypropylene, resin code 5, used for tubs, lids and food containers, is a recyclable plastic. Empty it and keep it with your dry waste.
PVC, resin code 3, is a recyclable resin on paper, but very few recyclers in India accept it and it is not safe to assume yours will. Worth asking locally rather than guessing.
Resin code 7 simply means other. It covers many unrelated plastics with no single answer between them, so there is no one rule to apply here.

rules.action: Dry waste, but not for recycling
rules.text: Multilayered packaging, such as a snack packet or a drink carton, bonds plastic, paper or foil into a single sheet that cannot be pulled apart again. The Plastic Waste Management Rules treat it as its own category rather than as a recyclable plastic.
Glass can be recycled over and over without losing quality. Empty it, keep it whole if you can, and keep it with your dry waste.
Aluminium is one of the most valuable things in your dry waste and is recycled again and again with very little loss. Empty it and keep it with your dry waste.
Steel and tin are pulled out magnetically during sorting, which makes them among the most reliably recycled materials. Empty it and keep it with your dry waste.
Corrugated cardboard is recycled readily as long as it stays dry. Flatten it, keep it away from your wet waste, and keep it dry until it is collected.
Clean dry paper is recycled readily. Once paper is wet or greasy the fibres are spoiled and it is no longer worth recycling, so keep it dry and away from your wet waste.
Nothing in this rule set covers that combination, so there is no cited rule to stand behind an answer. Checking it yourself beats a guess dressed up as a verdict.
